title: Magma and Lava
description: Where molten rock comes from and how it behaves

concepts.title: From Solid Rock to Magma
concepts.contentHtml:
Rock melts when heat, reduced pressure, or added water overcome the bonds holding its minerals together. Three settings trigger melting:

  • Decompression melting — rising mantle at mid-ocean ridges loses pressure and melts without getting hotter.
  • Flux melting — water released by subducting slabs lowers the melting point of the mantle above.
  • Heat-transfer melting — mantle plumes under hotspots bring enough heat to melt the overlying plate.

The resulting magma is less dense than solid rock, so it rises buoyantly — sometimes erupting as lava.

concepts.title: Magma Composition and Viscosity
concepts.contentHtml:
The most important property of magma is its viscosity — resistance to flow. Viscosity is mainly controlled by silica content and temperature:

  • Basaltic magma (~50 % SiO₂): low viscosity, high temperature (~1200 °C), flows easily.
  • Andesitic magma (~60 % SiO₂): intermediate.
  • Rhyolitic magma (~70 % SiO₂): very high viscosity, lower temperature (~800 °C), barely flows.

Viscosity determines eruption style. Runny basalt pours out gently; sticky rhyolite traps gases that build pressure until the volcano explodes.

concepts.title: Lava Types
concepts.contentHtml:
Once magma reaches the surface it is called lava. Geologists recognise distinct lava types by their texture:

Pahoehoe — smooth, ropy surface; forms when a thin, fast-moving basaltic lava develops a solid skin that wrinkles. Common in Hawaii.

A'a — rough, blocky, clinker-like surface; same basaltic composition but cooled and fragmented as it moved.

Pillow lava — rounded, pillow-shaped blobs that form when lava erupts underwater. The outer skin quenches rapidly, creating rounded forms. Most of Earth's ocean floor is covered in pillow lava.

title: Eruption Styles
description: Why some volcanoes ooze and others explode

concepts.title: Effusive vs Explosive Eruptions
concepts.contentHtml:
Eruption style is largely determined by magma viscosity and gas content. Two end members:

Effusive eruptions — low-viscosity basaltic magma lets gases escape gradually. Lava flows steadily from vents or fissures. Dangerous if you stand in the path, but rarely catastrophic. Hawaiian eruptions are the type example.

Explosive eruptions — high-viscosity silicic magma traps gases. Pressure builds until the magma shatters explosively, ejecting tephra (ash, pumice, blocks) high into the atmosphere. These can be catastrophic — Krakatoa (1883) was heard 4,800 km away.

concepts.title: The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI)
concepts.contentHtml:
The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measures eruption size on a logarithmic scale from 0 (gentle Hawaiian effusion) to 8 (supervolcanic caldera). Each step is roughly 10× the volume of erupted material.

Key events:
— Mount St. Helens 1980: VEI 5 (~1 km³)
— Pinatubo 1991: VEI 6 (~10 km³) — cooled global temperatures by ~0.5 °C for a year
— Tambora 1815: VEI 7 (~150 km³) — caused the 'Year Without a Summer' (1816)
— Yellowstone last eruption (640,000 years ago): VEI 8 (~1,000 km³)

concepts.title: Pyroclastic Flows and Surges
concepts.contentHtml:
The deadliest volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow — a fast-moving avalanche of hot gas, ash, and rock fragments that races down a volcano's flank at up to 700 km/h and temperatures of 500–1,000 °C. Nothing survives in its path.

The city of Pompeii was preserved in ash by Vesuvius's eruption in 79 CE, but the inhabitants of nearby Herculaneum were killed instantly by a pyroclastic surge. A 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée on Martinique sent a pyroclastic flow through the city of Saint-Pierre, killing ~30,000 people in minutes — one of history's worst volcanic disasters.

title: Volcano Types and Landforms
description: How different magmas build different mountains

concepts.title: Shield Volcanoes
concepts.contentHtml:
Shield volcanoes are built from successive flows of low-viscosity basaltic lava. They have broad, gently sloping profiles that resemble a warrior's shield laid flat — hence the name.

Mauna Loa in Hawaii is the largest active volcano on Earth by volume (about 80,000 km³) and rises over 9 km above the surrounding sea floor (neighbouring Mauna Kea is slightly taller). Its eruptions produce rivers of lava that can reach the sea but are rarely immediately lethal.

Shield volcanoes are also common on other planets: Olympus Mons on Mars is a shield volcano 22 km tall and 600 km wide — the largest known volcano in the Solar System.

concepts.title: Stratovolcanoes
concepts.contentHtml:
Stratovolcanoes (composite volcanoes) are the classic cone-shaped volcanoes of paintings and nightmares. They are built from alternating layers of lava flows and pyroclastic deposits — hence 'composite'.

Famous examples:
— Mount Vesuvius, Italy — destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 CE.
— Mount Fuji, Japan — perfectly symmetrical, last erupted in 1707.
— Krakatoa, Indonesia — its 1883 eruption killed ~36,000 people and sent a pressure wave around Earth four times.
— Mount St. Helens, USA — 1980 eruption removed the entire north flank in a lateral blast.

concepts.title: Calderas and Supervolcanoes
concepts.contentHtml:
A caldera forms when a magma chamber empties rapidly during a massive eruption and the ground above collapses inward. Calderas can be tens of kilometres wide — far larger than any cone a stratovolcano could build.

When a caldera-forming eruption exceeds VEI 8, ejecting more than 1,000 km³, the event is informally called a supervolcanic eruption. These are geological-scale catastrophes capable of triggering mass extinctions.

The Yellowstone caldera (Wyoming, USA) measures ~55 × 80 km. The most recent Yellowstone supereruption, 640,000 years ago, blanketed most of North America in ash. The caldera is still active, with ongoing uplift, geysers, and hot springs.

title: Famous Eruptions and Their Impacts
description: Case studies that shaped civilisations and climates

concepts.title: Tambora 1815 — A Global Climate Event
concepts.contentHtml:
The eruption of Mount Tambora on the island of Sumbawa, Indonesia in April 1815 was the largest eruption in recorded history (VEI 7). It killed ~71,000 people directly and ejected so much sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere that it reduced global temperatures by ~0.5–1 °C.

The following year, 1816, became known as the 'Year Without a Summer'. Crops failed across Europe and North America, causing widespread famine. The eerie red skies and cold summer in Switzerland reportedly inspired Mary Shelley to write Frankenstein and J.M.W. Turner's glowing sunsets in his paintings.

concepts.title: Krakatoa 1883 — Sound Heard Round the World
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa (Krakatau), Indonesia, was one of history's most violent volcanic events (VEI 6). The explosion generated the loudest sound ever recorded by humans — heard clearly 4,800 km away in Rodrigues Island near Mauritius, and faintly detected by barometers globally.

The eruption triggered a tsunami up to 30 m tall that killed ~36,000 people. The ash cloud circled Earth, producing vivid red sunsets worldwide for months and reducing global temperatures. The 1927 eruption in the caldera left behind a new island, Anak Krakatau ('Child of Krakatoa'), which remains active today.

concepts.title: Pompeii and Vesuvius — A Time Capsule
concepts.contentHtml:
The 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius preserved the Roman cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum under metres of volcanic ash and pyroclastic material — creating the most detailed snapshot of daily life in the ancient world.

Eyewitness accounts from Pliny the Younger describe the eruption column, darkness, and raining pumice. Modern geologists recognised this as a 'Plinian eruption' — a sustained column 30+ km tall — and named the style after Pliny.

Vesuvius is still active and today 3 million people live within its potential hazard zone. Emergency plans for a future eruption include evacuating the entire Naples region — one of the most complex disaster-preparedness challenges in the world.

title: Volcanoes and Earth Systems
description: How volcanism shapes climate, oceans, and life

concepts.title: Volcanism and the Atmosphere
concepts.contentHtml:
Earth's early atmosphere was largely produced by volcanic outgassing — volcanoes releasing water vapour, CO₂, nitrogen, and sulfur compounds from the interior over billions of years. The oceans themselves condensed from this volcanic water vapour.

Today, volcanism modulates climate on multiple timescales:
— Large eruptions inject sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, forming sulfate aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool the planet for 1–3 years.
— Over millions of years, sustained flood volcanism (large igneous provinces) releases enough CO₂ to drive significant warming — possibly contributing to several mass extinction events.

concepts.title: Large Igneous Provinces and Mass Extinctions
concepts.contentHtml:
A large igneous province (LIP) is an enormous outpouring of basaltic lava over a geologically short time. The Siberian Traps, erupted ~252 million years ago, covered 2 million km² and likely drove the Permian–Triassic mass extinction — the largest in Earth's history, killing ~96 % of marine species.

The Deccan Traps of India erupted around the same time as the asteroid impact 66 million years ago, and may have worsened the conditions that drove the end-Cretaceous mass extinction (which killed the non-avian dinosaurs).

LIPs demonstrate that volcanism, not just impacts, can reset the biosphere.

concepts.title: Volcanic Monitoring and Prediction
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern volcanology uses multiple techniques to anticipate eruptions:
— Seismicity — swarms of small earthquakes signal rising magma fracturing rock.
— Ground deformation — GPS and tiltmeters detect surface bulging as magma inflates the chamber.
— Gas emissions — increasing SO₂ and CO₂ flux from fumaroles indicates fresh magma degassing at depth.
— Thermal imaging — satellite data detects surface heat anomalies.

The 1991 Pinatubo eruption (VEI 6) was successfully forecast: 60,000 people were evacuated, saving tens of thousands of lives. Monitoring still cannot give precise timing, but it can give days to weeks of warning — enough to save lives.
